  • CASE STUDY ((20 Marks))
  • The Case: ZapCola's Jingle Problem.
  • • (2 Marks) may be given for general introduction to the case
  • i) Define consumer learning and explain, with reference to the case, how ZapCola's campaign
  • reflects principles of classical or operant conditioning. (Suggested allocation: (6 marks))
  • Suggested pointers for the answer: Marks
  • Consumer learning: The process by which consumers acquire purchase and consumption 2
  • knowledge and experience that they apply to future related behaviour.
  • Classical conditioning (in the case): The jingle was repeatedly 4
  • paired with ads and brand cues (unconditioned stimulus) until the consumer responded
  • with recall and liking; 68% could hum it. Repetition created the association.
  • Limits of conditioning / extinction: When the campaign paused, the pairing stopped and
  • recall fell to 11% (extinction / forgetting); the jingle was not linked to a usage occasion.
  • Suggested pointers for the answer: Marks
  • OR
  • Operant conditioning (in the case): Trial purchases were not reinforced by a strong 4
  • rewarding experience or cue, so habit did not form; FizzUp's repeated 'Sunday family
  • lunch' ritual reinforced repeat purchase.
  • ii) Distinguish between short-term memory (STM) and long-term memory (LTM). In your
  • opinion, why did the jingle create strong STM recall but weak LTM retention? (Suggested
  • allocation: (6 marks))
  • Suggested pointers for the answer: ((1 mark) may be awarded to each point) Marks
  • Distinction (any three points, (1 mark) each): STM: limited capacity (about 5 to 9 3
  • chunks), brief duration (seconds), temporary, holds current information, lost without
  • rehearsal. LTM: virtually unlimited capacity, durable and permanent storage, organised by
  • meaning, needs encoding and retrieval cues.
  • Why strong STM: A short, catchy, repeated five-second jingle is easy to attend to and 3
  • hold (rhythm, rehearsal by humming), giving immediate recall.
  • Why weak LTM: Shallow, repetitive encoding without meaning; no link to a usage
  • occasion or personal relevance (no elaborative rehearsal, no retrieval cue); no
  • reinforcement; decay and interference during the six-month pause; low involvement
  • purchase.
  • iii) Suggest two marketing strategies ZapCola could use to stimulate short-term memory and two
  • strategies to build long-term learning. (Suggested allocation: (6 marks).)
  • Suggested pointers for the answer
  • STM strategies (any two, (1.5 marks) each): Repetition and frequency of the jingle; short, simple
  • slogan or chunked message; distinctive sound, colour and visual cues; consistent placement (e.g., ad
  • ending); mnemonics and rhyme; high-impact attention-getting media bursts.
  • LTM strategies (any two, (1.5 marks) each): Link the brand to specific usage occasions through
  • storytelling (e.g., pizza, post-workout) as FizzUp did; emotional and elaborative messages; spaced
  • repetition over a long period; reinforcement through sampling, loyalty rewards and coupons; point-of
  • purchase cues near related products; brand rituals and consistent brand identity.
  • Note: This is an Apply/Analyse-based case study. Hence, marks may be awarded if students have been
  • able to successfully defend the answers based on the case study and additional knowledge about the
  • topic. Mark liberally.
  • General note: The pointers are suggestive. Any other relevant point or example given by the student may
  • be credited.

questions.question: Question 8
questions.solution_html:
• Performance review: Evaluating supplier performance to continue, modify or end the relationship.
  • 8b) A young professional purchases an expensive branded handbag because she believes it will
  • improve her social image and make her feel more confident. Identify the relevant buying motives
  • and explain how they influence her purchase decision.
  • Suggested pointers for the answer: (identification of motives (3 marks) for three relevant motives with
  • explanation; explanation of influence on decision (2 marks)) Mark liberally.
  • The young professional's purchase of an expensive branded handbag is primarily influenced by
  • emotional buying motives (such as prestige, status, self-esteem and self-confidence) and rational
  • motives (Quality, durability, brand reputation)
  • Emotional Motives
  • • Social image / prestige motive: Desire for status and approval from others; linked to esteem and
  • social needs (Maslow); conspicuous consumption.
  • • Confidence / self-esteem motive: Need to feel confident and enhance self-concept; the brand
  • acts as a symbol of identity.
  • • Social Acceptance Motive: The desire to create a favourable impression and gain recognition
  • from others may also influence her decision.
  • Rational / product-related motives
  • • Quality, durability, brand reputation and assurance (if mentioned).
  • How Buying Motives Influence Her Purchase Decision: Motives create the need, make social and
  • emotional attributes more important than price, and narrow evaluation to prestige brands.
  • Influence on Product Usage: Household size and composition determine the quantity and
  • types of products purchased. For example, a large family may prefer bulk grocery packs and
  • larger household appliances.
questions.final_answer: larger household appliances
questions.source_exam: V Semester MGU UGP (Honours) - 2024 Admission regular Examination October 2026

questions.question: Question 10
questions.solution_html:
• Importance for Market Segmentation: Marketers can use household size, family composition
  • and life cycle stages to identify consumer segments and develop suitable products and
  • promotional strategies. For example, companies may promote educational products to
  • families with school-going children.
  • Or Any other relevant point or example.
  • 9b) Analyse how the relative importance of internal and external influences varies across different
  • purchase situations. Discuss the influence of personal factors, psychological factors, family
  • reference groups, culture, social class and marketing stimuli on high-involvement and low
  • involvement purchase decisions, with suitable examples.
  • Introduction and Explaining Internal and external factors and Involvement ((8 marks))
  • • Consumer buying behaviour is influenced by a combination of internal and external factors.
  • Internal influences arise from the individual consumer, while external influences originate from
  • the consumer's social, cultural and marketing environment.
  • • Internal influences include personal factors such as age, income, occupation, lifestyle and
  • personality, and psychological factors such as motivation, perception, learning, attitudes and
  • beliefs.
  • • External influences include family, reference groups, culture, social class and marketing stimuli
  • such as product features, price, advertising and promotional offers.
  • The relative importance of these influences varies according to the level of consumer involvement, the
  • nature of the product, the perceived risk and the purchase situation.
  • High-involvement purchases: decisions in which consumers invest considerable time and effort because
  • the product is expensive, personally important, unfamiliar or associated with significant risk. Consumers
  • usually engage in extensive information search and careful evaluation. Example: Purchasing a car
  • selecting a college, buying a house or choosing a health insurance policy.
  • Low-involvement purchases are routine decisions involving relatively little perceived risk, financial
  • commitment or personal importance. Consumers generally make these purchases quickly, often relying
  • on habits, familiarity and convenience. Example: Purchasing toothpaste, biscuits, soap, salt or a familiar
  • brand of packaged food.
  • The importance of internal and external factors differs between these two types of purchases.
  • Comparative Analysis of Internal and External Influences
  • Influencing High-Involvement Purchase Decisions Low-Involvement Purchase Decisions
  • Factor
questions.final_answer: Factor

  • reference groups, culture, social class and marketing stimuli on high-involvement and low
  • involvement purchase decisions, with suitable examples.
  • Introduction and Explaining Internal and external factors and Involvement ((8 marks))
  • • Consumer buying behaviour is influenced by a combination of internal and external factors.
  • Internal influences arise from the individual consumer, while external influences originate from
  • the consumer's social, cultural and marketing environment.
  • • Internal influences include personal factors such as age, income, occupation, lifestyle and
  • personality, and psychological factors such as motivation, perception, learning, attitudes and
  • beliefs.
  • • External influences include family, reference groups, culture, social class and marketing stimuli
  • such as product features, price, advertising and promotional offers.
  • The relative importance of these influences varies according to the level of consumer involvement, the
  • nature of the product, the perceived risk and the purchase situation.
  • High-involvement purchases: decisions in which consumers invest considerable time and effort because
  • the product is expensive, personally important, unfamiliar or associated with significant risk. Consumers
  • usually engage in extensive information search and careful evaluation. Example: Purchasing a car
  • selecting a college, buying a house or choosing a health insurance policy.
  • Low-involvement purchases are routine decisions involving relatively little perceived risk, financial
  • commitment or personal importance. Consumers generally make these purchases quickly, often relying
  • on habits, familiarity and convenience. Example: Purchasing toothpaste, biscuits, soap, salt or a familiar
  • brand of packaged food.
  • The importance of internal and external factors differs between these two types of purchases.
